❯ [Speech] What hardware do you need?                                           

  Thought for 55s (ctrl+o to expand)

● Python, not Rust or C. And the hardware you already have is enough to start.

  Language. Building a voice model means fine-tuning an existing open
  voice-cloning model on recordings of you, not writing one from scratch. Every
  credible open model for this, such as XTTS-v2, F5-TTS, Fish Speech, CosyVoice
  and Chatterbox, ships as PyTorch code with Python training scripts. Choosing
  Rust means reimplementing the model, the neural audio codec and the training
  loop yourself, with no upstream to lean on. C is worse still, with no autograd
  and no model zoo. Most of the actual work is data preparation and evaluation
  anyway: transcribing, segmenting and cleaning your audio, and all of that
  tooling is Python too.

  Rust has one legitimate place here, and it comes later. Once the voice sounds
  right, you can export the model to ONNX and serve inference from a small
  single binary with no Python runtime. That is a nice-to-have for deployment,
  not a reason to build in Rust. I'd leave it out until the voice is good.

  This is a one-way-door decision, so it should be recorded as an ADR. Confirm
  Python and I'll file it.

  Hardware. This machine can do it. The card is the constraint, and it sets
  which route you take.

  ┌──────────┬─────────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────────────────┐
  │ Resource │  This machine   │  Zero-shot    │        Fine-tuning         │
  │          │                 │    cloning    │                            │
  ├──────────┼─────────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
  │ GPU VRAM │ 8 GB (RTX 2060  │ Plenty        │ Tight but workable with    │
  │          │ SUPER)          │               │ small batches              │
  ├──────────┼─────────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
  │ RAM      │ 31 GB           │ Fine          │ Fine                       │
  ├──────────┼─────────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────────────────┤
  │ Disk     │ Not checked     │ ~5 GB per     │ ~5 GB per model            │
  │          │                 │ model         │                            │
  └──────────┴─────────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────────────────┘

  Zero-shot cloning needs a short clip of you and runs comfortably on this card.
  It gets you a recognisable voice in an afternoon. Fine-tuning gets much
  closer to you and needs more recordings. If 8 GB proves too tight for the
  model we pick, a rented 24 GB GPU costs a few pounds for the whole fine-tune
  run, so I would not buy hardware for this.

  The hardware that matters most is not the GPU. It is a decent microphone and a
  quiet room. Data quality dominates model quality. For zero-shot, under a
  minute of clean speech. For fine-tuning, somewhere between twenty minutes and
  two hours of varied read speech, recorded cleanly. Beyond that, returns
  diminish quickly for a single voice.

  The next decision after language is which model to fine-tune, and that one
  should be settled empirically: record a small sample, run two or three
  candidates on it, and pick by ear.

  Microphone

  Your RØDE VideoMic GO II is already working: plugged in, detected, set as the
  default input, capturing 48 kHz 24-bit mono, and shared with your vtt-linux
  dictation tool through PipeWire. I took a three-second ambient sample to check

  ┌─────────────────────┬────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
  │     Measurement     │ Value  │    Target for training data    │
  ├─────────────────────┼────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Ambient noise, mean │ -44 dB │ below -50 dB                   │
  ├─────────────────────┼────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Ambient noise, peak │ -32 dB │ below -40 dB                   │
  ├─────────────────────┼────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Input gain          │ 0.97   │ set by the speaking test below │
  └─────────────────────┴────────┴────────────────────────────────┘

  The room is noisier than we want, probably the PC fans. The VideoMic GO II is
  a shotgun mic, so it rejects noise from the sides and rear well if it is
  pointed at your mouth. Positioning will do more than any software fix.

  1. Fit the foam windshield and aim the mic at your mouth from about 20 cm, 
  pointing away from the PC

  Expected: the foam is the pop filter for this mic. Close-miking without it
  puts plosives on every "p" and "b" in the training data.

  2. Run the speaking test while reading a sentence or two at normal volume

  timeout 10 pw-record --rate 48000 --channels 1 --format s16
  /tmp/level-test.wav; ffmpeg -hide_banner -i /tmp/level-test.wav -af
  volumedetect -f null - 2>&1 | grep -E 'mean_volume|max_volume'

  - max_volume between -12 dB and -6 dB → continue to step 3
  - max_volume above -1 dB → clipping; run wpctl set-volume 
    @DEFAULT_AUDIO_SOURCE@ 0.7 and redo step 2
  - max_volume below -20 dB → too quiet; move closer and redo step 2

  3. Run the silence test with your hands off the keyboard

  timeout 5 pw-record --rate 48000 --channels 1 --format s16
  /tmp/silence-test.wav; ffmpeg -hide_banner -i /tmp/silence-test.wav -af
  volumedetect -f null - 2>&1 | grep mean_volume

  - mean_volume below -50 dB → good, recording can start
  - mean_volume above -50 dB → move the mic further from the PC or turn the fans
    down, redo step 3

  4. Listen back

  pw-play /tmp/level-test.wav

  Expected: you hear yourself clearly with no hum, hiss or popping.

  Shortlist for the bake-off

  1. Chatterbox (Resemble AI), 500M standard / 350M Turbo. MIT for both code and
     weights. Best-evidenced zero-shot clone of 2026 and small enough to run
     FP32 on 8 GB. Fine-tune is a community LoRA toolkit, not first-party.
  2. F5-TTS, ~335M. The only shortlist entry with an official first-party
     fine-tuning app and training scripts. MIT code, CC-BY-NC weights, so
     personal use only. ONNX port exists.
  3. Orpheus TTS, 3B, Apache 2.0. Highest fidelity ceiling, official finetune
     config plus Unsloth notebooks, and Q8 GGUF inference at ~4 GB gives you the
     llama.cpp and Rust path. Training needs the rented GPU.

  CosyVoice 3 is the named alternate. Breeze TTS 2 tops the open-weight
  leaderboard but needs 12 GB and has no fine-tune path at all.

  Zero-shot baseline: Chatterbox standard, from 60 seconds of reference audio,
  today. The accent-follows-the-reference behaviour is documented rather than
  hoped for.

  Top three gotchas

● epc-voice — The Quest

  Come, let me tell you what this project is for. Emmanuel's voice is fully
  reproducible from text: anything he writes can be heard spoken in his own
  voice, achieved with Claude's help. That is the vision, and the mission
  underneath it is plain — collect recordings of Emmanuel's voice, train or
  fine-tune a text-to-speech model on them, and iterate until text input is
  spoken as Emmanuel. The project vows to reproduce his voice faithfully from
  text, and to use that voice only with his knowledge and consent. Both halves
  of that vow matter. A voice clone that nobody can tell from the real thing is
  exactly as dangerous as it is useful, and the roadmap treats the second half
  as engineering work rather than as a good intention.

  Five decisions shape how this gets built, and each one closed a door on
  purpose. The training pipeline is Python 3.12 managed with uv, because every
  credible open voice-cloning model ships as PyTorch code with Python training
  scripts, and Rust — which Emmanuel already ships a voice-to-text product in —
  would mean reimplementing the model, the codec and the training loop with no
  upstream to lean on. The harness never imports a model: each candidate lives
  in its own uv project under models/, reached through a subprocess contract,
  because the three shortlisted models pin conflicting versions of torch and
  would otherwise take each other down. Inference runs locally in float32 or a
  quantised runtime and never in half precision, because the RTX 2060 SUPER is a
  Turing card with no bfloat16, no FlashAttention 2, and a filed report of NaNs
  in generation on this exact card class; every fine-tune therefore runs on a
  rented Ampere spot instance, logged to a cost file, under a twenty-pound cap.
  Quality is gated on Emmanuel's own real-versus-real similarity range rather
  than any fixed threshold, because there is no universal number and a made-up
  one would be arbitrary or wrong — if the clone sits inside the range his own
  recordings occupy, it is as much him as his own speech is. And emotion, accent
  and language travel as a closed-vocabulary style tag on every corpus row and
  every prompt, mapped per adapter, because Chatterbox, F5-TTS and Orpheus each
  control tone in incompatible ways and without one vocabulary the corpus, the
  prompts and the adapters would quietly drift apart.

  Nothing has been built yet. [DIRECT-EV001 p0] Build Emmanuel's voice clone —
  text in, Emmanuel's voice out, indistinguishable from him is in progress,
  thirty-three tasks across four features, and every one of them is upcoming.
  What follows is the quest as planned, not as fought.

  The first thread, and the one everything else hangs from, is [STORY-EV001] any
  text spoken in my own voice so that everything I write can be heard as me,
  delivering [FEAT-EV001 p0 must-have] Text to Emmanuel's voice — local
  text-to-speech in Emmanuel's cloned voice, indistinguishable from him to
  people who know him. It begins where it has to: [TASK-EV008 p0] Scaffold the
  Python harness project, the only task with nothing blocking it, because the
  module names it fixes are the names every later task writes against. From
  there the work fans out. [TASK-EV009 p0] Build the recording kit gives
  Emmanuel level and silence checks before a single take, so a noisy room is
  caught while it is still cheap to fix rather than baked into training data.
  [TASK-EV010 p0] Build the corpus preparation pipeline turns takes into clips
  of three to fifteen seconds, trims the trailing silence that causes runaway
  generation, normalises loudness because inconsistent levels measurably degrade
  speaker similarity, and transcribes with Whisper for hand correction —
  because a transcript that does not match what was actually said is the single
  most-cited cause of mispronunciation. [TASK-EV011 p0] Author the fixed test
  sets and ABX protocol writes the prompts everything is scored on. [TASK-EV012
  p0] Build the similarity, WER and naturalness scorers loads two speaker
  embedders rather than one, since the 2026 evidence shows they disagree about
  which clone sounds more like its speaker. Alongside them, [TASK-EV016 p1]
  Write the cloud GPU runbook and cost log makes renting a GPU a script rather
  than a console session, and [TASK-EV033 p2] Add local pre-commit checks makes

  Right now that archive holds 2.5 minutes. The sample rate is the part that
  matters: the models train at 24 kHz, and upsampling cannot invent the 8 to 16
  kHz band where sibilance and breath live. That band is part of why a voice
  sounds like a person, so a 16 kHz corpus would cap you below "scary good".

  All three are fixable inside your own tool, and the resample path already
  exists for devices that cannot open 16 kHz. So TASK-EV034 (Extend
  voice-to-text to archive training-grade audio) captures at 48 kHz, downsamples
  to 16 kHz at the Whisper call only, archives with a JSON sidecar carrying the
  transcript, and keeps the whole thing opt-in and off by default since that
  tool is public. TASK-EV035 (Build the dictation corpus importer) brings it
  into the corpus with a denylist and a 10% hand-checked sample rather than
  correcting every line.

  On candid versus performed, you are right and it cuts both ways. Candid speech
  is exactly what the research says fools someone who knows you, so the bulk of
  the corpus being dictation is an advantage, not a compromise. What dictation
  cannot give is phonetic balance, questions and exclamations, and the eight
  emotional styles, because you do not dictate in a whisper or a newsreader
  voice. So the plan is now hybrid: dictation supplies the hours, and your
  deliberate recording drops from two hours to under one, split into a 45-minute

  once, then whatever you dictate anyway.

● epc-voice — The Quest

  Come, let me tell you what this project is for. Emmanuel's voice is fully
  reproducible from text: anything he writes can be heard spoken in his own
  voice, achieved with Claude's help. That is the vision, and the mission
  underneath it is plain — collect recordings of Emmanuel's voice, train or
  fine-tune a text-to-speech model on them, and iterate until text input is
  spoken as Emmanuel. The project vows to reproduce his voice faithfully from
  text, and to use that voice only with his knowledge and consent. Both halves
  of that vow matter, and the second is engineering work, not a good intention:
  a written policy, a token on the server, weights that never leave this
  machine.

  Six decisions shape how this gets built, and each closed a door on purpose.
  The training pipeline is Python 3.12 with uv, because every credible open
  voice-cloning model ships as PyTorch code with Python training scripts, and
  Rust — which Emmanuel already ships a voice-to-text product in — would mean
  reimplementing the model, the codec and the training loop with no upstream to
  lean on. The harness never imports a model: each candidate lives in its own uv
  project under models/, reached through a subprocess contract, because the
  three shortlisted models pin conflicting torch versions and would otherwise
  take each other down. Inference runs locally in float32 or a quantised
  runtime, never half precision, because the RTX 2060 SUPER is a Turing card
  with a filed report of NaNs in generation on this exact card class; every
  fine-tune therefore runs on a rented Ampere spot instance, logged to a cost
  file, under a twenty-pound cap. Quality is gated on Emmanuel's own
  real-versus-real similarity range rather than any fixed threshold, because
  there is no universal number and a made-up one would be arbitrary — a clone
  that sits inside the range his own recordings occupy is as much him as his own
  speech is. Emotion, accent and language travel as a closed-vocabulary style
  tag on every corpus row and every prompt, mapped per adapter, because the
  three candidates control tone in incompatible ways and one vocabulary keeps
  them from drifting apart. And, decided only hours ago, the corpus is hybrid:
  dictation — audio Emmanuel already produces all day talking to his computer —
  supplies the bulk and grows passively, while deliberate recording shrinks to
  under an hour and covers only what dictation cannot give: phonetic balance,
  questions and exclamations, the eight emotional styles, and any accent he
  chooses to perform.

  Nothing has shipped yet. [DIRECT-EV001 p0] Build Emmanuel's voice clone — text
  in, Emmanuel's voice out, indistinguishable from him is in progress, four
  features and thirty-five tasks under it, and all but one of those tasks is
  upcoming. The one exception is [TASK-EV034 p0] Extend voice-to-text to archive
  training-grade audio, in progress right now under a session dedicated to that
  sibling repository — a collision on this very file, caught and handed off
  cleanly rather than fought over, with the handoff itself now part of this
  project's working record.

  The first and largest thread is [STORY-EV001] any text spoken in my own voice
  so that everything I write can be heard as me, delivering [FEAT-EV001 p0
  must-have] Text to Emmanuel's voice — local text-to-speech in Emmanuel's
  cloned voice, indistinguishable from him to people who know him. It begins
  where it has to: [TASK-EV008 p0] Scaffold the Python harness project, the only
  task nothing blocks, because the module names it fixes are the names every
  later task writes against. Running beside it, unblocked by anything, is
  [TASK-EV034 p0] Extend voice-to-text to archive training-grade audio itself —
  the dictation tool's capture moves from 16 kHz to 48 kHz, because upsampling
  later could never invent back the missing octave of sibilance and breath, and
  every recording gets archived with its transcript, opt-in and off by default
  in a tool other people use too.

  From the scaffold, four cards fan out in parallel: [TASK-EV009 p0] Build the
  recording kit gives Emmanuel level and silence checks before a single take.
  [TASK-EV011 p0] Author the fixed test sets and ABX protocol writes the prompts
  everything is scored on. [TASK-EV012 p0] Build the similarity, WER and
  naturalness scorers loads two disagreeing speaker embedders rather than
  trusting one, because the 2026 evidence shows they judge likeness differently.
  And [TASK-EV016 p1] Write the cloud GPU runbook and cost log turns renting a
  GPU into a script rather than a console session. [TASK-EV009] itself now waits
  one step longer than it first appeared to — on [TASK-EV011], because its own
  smoke test reads a prompt file only that card produces, a gap an independent
  audit caught and this roadmap has since closed.

  Then two corpora converge. Emmanuel records [TASK-EV001 p0] the deliberate
  seed corpus — a session of about twenty minutes, all the smaller for what
  dictation now carries instead. [TASK-EV010 p0] Build the corpus preparation
  pipeline turns any recording into clips of three to fifteen seconds, trims the
  silence that causes runaway generation, and transcribes for hand correction,
  because a transcript that does not match what was actually said is the single
  most-cited cause of mispronunciation. The two meet at [TASK-EV017 p0] Prepare
  the seed corpus and carve the holdout, which builds the corpus and cuts free a
  slice that trains nothing and never becomes a reference — the real side of
  every score and every blind test to come. Beside it, the moment recordings
  exist, [TASK-EV025 p0] Back up the corpus and weights privately runs encrypted
  and off this machine, because the recordings are the one thing here that
  cannot be remade cheaply. And [TASK-EV035 p0], built on the archiving change,
  imports the dictation Emmanuel has already produced — hand-checking only a
  sample of its transcripts rather than every line, and feeding straight into
  the full corpus that follows.

  Only then does a voice appear. [TASK-EV003 p0] Build the Chatterbox adapter
  and zero-shot baseline clones Emmanuel from sixty seconds of audio with no
  training at all — the floor every fine-tune must beat, and the first time the
  whole pipeline runs end to end. What happens next is a bake-off, not a bet,
  and this is where the project's own quiet correction shows most clearly: an
  independent audit checked every claim about the tools these three cards depend
  on against their live source, and three of them turned out wrong. [TASK-EV013
  p1] Fine-tune Chatterbox with LoRA on the seed corpus assumed a training
  script that takes command-line flags; it does not — it reads a config file, so
  the card now patches that file directly, and a merge step once written as a
  contingency turns out to be mandatory, not optional. [TASK-EV015 p1] Build the
  Orpheus adapter with LoRA fine-tune and GGUF inference pointed its
  instructions at a README that does not exist in the fine-tuning folder; the
  fix names the three files that are actually there. None of these were guesses
  corrected by another guess — each was checked against the tool's own
  repository and fixed with a citation. [TASK-EV014 p1] Build the F5-TTS adapter
  and fine-tune on the seed corpus runs alongside them, and all three now write
  to the same shared cost ledger safely, appending under a lock rather than
  racing each other's running total. [TASK-EV004 p1] Compare the bake-off
  results and decide the model closes the fan-out with a decision rule written
  before the numbers exist, gated now on a British-accent check as well as on
  similarity, and records the answer as an architectural decision rather than a
  preference.

  After the decision, the corpus grows once more. [TASK-EV005 p1] Record the
  styled and top-up sessions is where the second thread joins the first, and it
  was quietly broken until this week: it asked for eight emotional styles but
  every style shared one session and one set of prompt ids, so only the first
  style would ever have actually been recorded — a defect an audit surfaced
  before a single minute was lost, not after. [TASK-EV006 p1] Fine-tune the
  chosen model and run the blind test is the moment [FEAT-EV001] either closes
  or names exactly what is missing: a blind test where familiar listeners do no
  better than chance. [TASK-EV007 p1] Wire the voice into the F9 reader — raised
  this week from a lower priority once it became clear a later card cannot
  harden a server that does not yet exist — puts the finished voice where
  Emmanuel will actually use it, sharing one sentence-splitter with the
  long-form reader that comes later rather than each reimplementing its own.

  The second thread asks a question of its own. [STORY-EV002] my voice to carry
  the emotion and tone I ask for so that a story, a warning and a joke do not
  all sound the same delivers [FEAT-EV002 p1 performance] Emotion and tone on
  demand. Eight styles — neutral, warm, excited, sombre, urgent, whisper,
  storytelling, newsreader — become tags on the data and the prompts, recorded
  inside the same session as the top-up rather than a separate sitting.
  [TASK-EV018 p1] Build the emotion and style evaluation fits its judgement to
  Emmanuel's own styled recordings, so the ceiling it measures against is his
  real voice, not a generic emotion model's opinion — and it now properly
  depends on the segmentation code it actually calls, a gap the same audit
  closed. [TASK-EV019 p1] Implement style control in the chosen adapter maps
  each tag honestly, declaring in its own output any style a model cannot carry
  rather than hiding the gap.

  The third thread is about not sounding like somebody else. [STORY-EV003] my
  voice to stay British in English and to speak other languages and accents
  convincingly delivers [FEAT-EV003 p2 performance] British accent preserved,
  names pronounced right, and Emmanuel's voice in other languages and
  performable accents. No public benchmark measures British preservation for any
  open model, so [TASK-EV020 p1] Build the accent fidelity evaluation has to
  build the measurement before it can report a result — and that result now
  feeds directly into the bake-off's own decision rule, so a candidate that
  drifts American cannot win regardless of how it scores elsewhere. [TASK-EV021
  p2] Evaluate cross-lingual synthesis in Emmanuel's voice takes his timbre into
  two other languages, and here too the audit found a real gap: the
  multilingual engine validates its language codes strictly, lowercase and bare,
  and the card now says so rather than assuming a format that would have
  silently rejected every request. [TASK-EV022 p3] Record and evaluate an accent
  sub-corpus is the honest limit of the whole thread — the model reproduces
  only what the corpus contains, so an accent on demand means Emmanuel
  performing it on tape first.

  The fourth thread is what separates a trained voice from a kept one.
  [STORY-EV004] the voice kept safe, versioned and improvable over time delivers
  [FEAT-EV004 p1 must-have] Voice stewardship. [TASK-EV024 p1] Build the
  checkpoint registry and regression suite makes promotion a measured decision,
  never a feeling about which take sounded nicer. [TASK-EV026 p1] Write the
  voice use policy and harden the server turns the vow into enforcement — a
  policy Emmanuel signs, a token, a request log that keeps a hash and never the
  words themselves. [TASK-EV028 p2] Write the retraining runbook and [TASK-EV031
  p3] Run the quarterly drift check and maintain the voice both learned the
  same lesson from the same audit: each assumed a status check that only a
  still-unbuilt runbook card actually provides, and both now wait on it
  properly. And [TASK-EV032 p3] Export to ONNX and build the Rust inference
  binary finally opens the door the language decision deliberately left shut — a
  Python-free reader, proven equal to the Python original before it is trusted
  with anything.

  Where this is going: one voice Emmanuel can hand any text, in any of eight
  tones, in his own accent or a couple of others, and hear himself say it — on
  his own machine, the weights backed up, the policy signed, and a regression
  check standing between any future change and the voice he approved.
  Thirty-five tasks, none of them done, all of them immediately workable — there
  is no backlog here, no work parked for later, because a project this size on
  its first day has nothing yet worth deferring. Layer zero holds two cards and
  both are startable now.

          et dictation]`; `epc-voice prep review-sample --corpus data/cor
          pus/dictation --fraction 0.10`; `epc-voice prep apply` already 
          exists and applies the corrections.
      46  
      47 +## Archive contract                                            
      48 +                                                               
      49 +Verified 2026-09-03 against the voice-to-text implementation (`
         +src/archive.rs`, `src/settings.rs`, README) at commit 4d18734, 
         +not against its task card. Four points diverge from the assumpt
         +ions this card was first written with, and each one silently pr
         +oduces zero imported clips rather than an error:               
      50 +                                                               
      51 +- **Root is `~/.config/voice-to-text/archive`**, not `~/.local/
         +share/…`. `resolve_archive_dir` defaults to `config_dir.join("a
         +rchive")`; an empty `archive_dir` setting means beside the conf
         +ig, and a `~/`-prefixed value expands against home. Only the lo
         +gs and the debug ring live under `~/.local/share/`.            
      52 +- **Layout is one directory per day**: `<archive_dir>/<YYYY-MM-
         +DD>/vtt_<id>.wav` plus `vtt_<id>.json`. A flat glob of the root
         + finds nothing — recurse one level. Ids are timestamp-shaped (`
         +vtt_20260903T034812_123`), so stems sort chronologically and `-
         +-since` can filter on the directory name without opening a file
         +.                                                              
      53 +- **The archive is capped and self-pruning.** `archive_max_file
         +s` defaults to 5000 (roughly 11 hours, under a gigabyte), delet
         +ing oldest-first across dated directories with wav and sidecar 
         +removed together; `0` means unbounded. Files therefore disappea
         +r between runs: import incrementally and treat a missing item a
         +s normal, never as an error.                                   
      54 +- **Sidecar keys** are `id`, `recorded_at` (RFC3339 with offset
         +), `duration_s` (float, 3dp), `sample_rate` (int), `text`, `mod
         +el`, `language`, `app` (string or null; null today). There is n
         +o wav path field — pair by stem.                               
      55 +                                                               
      56 +Never read `~/.local/share/voice-to-text/recordings/`. That is 
         +a 20-file debug ring feeding the tray's re-transcribe-last reco
         +very net; it is 16 kHz by design and stays that way, because `w
         +hisper::decode_wav_to_samples` rejects any other rate.         
      57 +                                                               
      58 +Capture is 48 kHz mono, resampled to 16 kHz at the end of `stop
         +_recording` so Whisper receives the rate it always did. Bit dep
         +th is 16-bit at 4d18734 and moving to 24-bit to match this repo
         +'s audio conventions — TASK-EV034 (Extend voice-to-text to arch
         +ive training-grade audio) said 16-bit in its Interfaces section
         + while AGENTS.md says 24-bit, and the divergence is being resol
         +ved in favour of AGENTS.md while no archive exists to migrate. 
      59 +                                                               
      60 +The archive is off by default (`archive=1` in `~/.config/voice-
         +to-text/settings.conf`) and the feature is unreleased — Cargo.t
         +oml on main still reads 2.3.11, which is also the installed PPA
         + version, so a local build is required before any data accumula
         +tes.

          nd `AGENTS.md`, alongside `seed`, `full` and `holdout`.

  I was wrong last turn. I measured ~/.local/share/voice-to-text/recordings/ and
  called it the archive. It's a 20-file debug ring that feeds the tray's
  re-transcribe-last recovery net — 16 kHz by design, permanently. The 48 kHz
  capture already shipped at commit 4d18734. My "EV034 is a bigger change than
  it looks" was built on that mistake; disregard it.

  But checking their reply against the code found one thing that would have cost
  us silently. They told me the archive defaults to
  ~/.local/share/voice-to-text/archive. It doesn't:

  if trimmed.is_empty() {
      return config_dir.join("archive");
  }

  The default is ~/.config/voice-to-text/archive — their own README says so
  twice. My importer was pointed at the wrong directory and would have found
  nothing, reporting zero imported minutes rather than an error. Fixed, along
  with three more things they volunteered that I hadn't asked about: the archive
  is one directory per day (a flat glob finds nothing), it's capped at 5000 
  files and self-prunes oldest-first (so files vanish between runs and absence
  must be normal, not an error), and the sidecar carries eight named keys paired
  by stem. All now written into TASK-EV035 (Build the dictation corpus
  importer) and committed as 6b23578 — checks green.

  The real lever is you, and it's two commands. The feature is on main but
  unreleased: apt-cache policy voice-to-text reports Installed 2.3.11, Candidate
  2.3.11, and Cargo.toml on main is also 2.3.11 — so apt update cannot deliver
  it. You need a local build.

  then shows something newer than 2.3.11.

  vtt_<id>.wav + .json pairs as you dictate.

  then isn't recoverable. At the 5000-file default the archive settles around 11
  hours of audio, under a gigabyte.

  section says 48 kHz 16-bit while AGENTS.md says 24-bit. The peer is switching
